cards.front: Why is an international treaty needed to phase out ozone-depleting substances?
cards.back: Chemicals drift across borders, so no single country can fix the problem alone. The **Montreal Protocol** (1987) gave nations a shared treaty to phase them out.
cards.hint: Think about where the chemicals go after they are released.

cards.front: What makes a good substitute for a CFC?
cards.back: A good substitute avoids **chlorine and bromine**, and it should also be safe, affordable, and efficient. Each option trades one concern for another.
cards.hint: Compare the substitutes in the table with the CFCs they replace.

cards.front: Why will the ozone layer take decades to recover even after CFC production stops?
cards.back: CFCs have a long **atmospheric lifetime**, so chlorine keeps reaching the stratosphere. Old equipment and foam still hold CFCs that can leak.
A **human-made chemical**, such as a CFC or halon, that releases chlorine or bromine in the stratosphere and destroys ozone.

cards.front: What is a phase-out in the context of ozone-depleting substances?
cards.back: A **planned, gradual end** to the production and use of a substance. It gives industries time to switch to other products.
cards.hint: Think about what industries need before a ban takes full effect.

cards.front: How can coolant be kept out of the air when old refrigerators and air conditioners are repaired or scrapped?
cards.back: Technicians use **refrigerant recovery** to capture the coolant for reuse or destruction, instead of venting it into the air.
cards.hint: Think about what happens to equipment at repair or disposal time.

cards.front: What mistake do students often make about stopping new production of CFCs?
cards.back: They assume it stops releases at once. **Old equipment and stored stocks** can still leak, so releases continue after production ends.

cards.front: How did the Montreal Protocol treat developing countries?
cards.back: It gave them **longer deadlines** and financial help to adopt substitutes, because switching takes time and money.
cards.hint: Think about what switching to substitutes costs.

cards.front: How does an HFC differ from an HCFC as a substitute for CFCs?
cards.back: An HFC contains **no chlorine**, so it does not destroy ozone, though many trap heat strongly. An HCFC still contains chlorine and harms ozone, though less than a CFC.
cards.hint: Look at which elements each compound contains.

cards.front: What do ammonia, carbon dioxide, and propane have in common as substitutes?
cards.back: They contain **no chlorine, fluorine, or bromine**. Each still has a concern: ammonia is toxic if leaked, carbon dioxide needs high-pressure systems, and propane is flammable.

cards.front: How do scientists track whether the ozone layer is recovering?
cards.back: They measure **stratospheric chlorine** and **Antarctic ozone** each spring. Levels of chlorine-containing chemicals have fallen since the treaty took effect.
cards.hint: Think about what is measured and when.

cards.front: Why was a later amendment to the Montreal Protocol needed for HFCs?
cards.back: Many HFCs trap heat strongly, so a **later amendment** phases down HFCs. Substitutes can create new problems.
cards.hint: Consider the side effects of the substitutes.

cards.front: What made the ozone case a success, according to the note?
cards.back: Countries agreed on a **clear target**, had substitutes available, and shared costs. Production of the main ozone-depleting substances has fallen sharply.
